eras.name: Roots: Ragtime & Blues
eras.tagline: Ragtime, the blues and the brass bands that came first
eras.summary:
Before anyone called it jazz, America was already humming its ingredients. Ragtime pianists syncopated their right hands against a left hand that marched like a brass band, and Scott Joplin gave the style a composer's poise, publishing rags with the care of a European art-song writer. Across the South, the blues carried a different truth: bent notes, call-and-response and a twelve-bar shape sturdy enough to hold any story.

New Orleans was where those currents collided. Brass bands played funerals and parades, Creole musicians brought conservatory polish, and cornetists like Buddy Bolden loosened the rhythm until it began to rock. The city's dance halls and street corners became a laboratory for collective improvisation, years before a single jazz note was recorded.

What survives of this era reaches us through sheet music, piano rolls and the first blues records cut by the women who had sung this music in tent shows for years. Listen past the crackle and you will hear the DNA of everything that follows: the blue notes, the rhythmic push and pull, and the habit of turning a fixed melody into a personal statement.

eras.name: New Orleans & the Jazz Age
eras.tagline: Hot jazz, Satchmo and the Roaring Twenties
eras.summary:
In 1917 a white New Orleans group, the Original Dixieland Jass Band, cut the first jazz record in New York, and the music went national almost overnight. The deeper story belonged to the Black and Creole players who had built the style: King Oliver, Jelly Roll Morton, Sidney Bechet and, above all, a young cornetist named Louis Armstrong. As the Great Migration pulled musicians north, Chicago's South Side became jazz's second home.

The early bands worked in polyphony, with the cornet leading, the clarinet weaving filigree around it and the trombone growling underneath. Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven records blew that model open. His solos had the architecture of a great speech, and his phrasing taught the whole world what swing could feel like. Bix Beiderbecke offered a cooler, bell-like lyricism, while Harlem stride pianists turned ragtime into a two-fisted athletic display.

This was the Jazz Age of speakeasies, radio, dance crazes and the first star soloists. By the time the stock market crashed, jazz had grown from a regional folk music into the soundtrack of a modern nation.

eras.name: The Swing Era
eras.tagline: Big bands, ballrooms and America's popular music
eras.summary:
For roughly a decade and a half, jazz was simply America's pop music. Big bands of fourteen or more players filled ballrooms from the Savoy in Harlem to the Palomar in Los Angeles, and the rhythm smoothed into a buoyant four-to-the-bar pulse built for dancing. Arrangers became as important as soloists, writing call-and-response riffs between brass and reed sections that could lift a room off its feet.

Duke Ellington turned the orchestra into a composer's palette, writing for the specific voices of his players. Count Basie's Kansas City band proved that less could be more, riding a feather-light rhythm section and blues riffs. Benny Goodman was crowned the King of Swing and integrated his small groups when that was a radical act. Out front, tenor giants Coleman Hawkins and Lester Young, and singers like Billie Holiday and Ella Fitzgerald, defined what it meant to interpret a song.

Swing was global, too: in Paris, Django Reinhardt fused Romani guitar with Armstrong's lessons. Wartime travel limits, a long recording ban and changing tastes eventually thinned the big bands, but their language of riffs, ballads and blues remains the common tongue of jazz.

eras.name: Bebop
eras.tagline: Speed, wit and the birth of modern jazz
eras.summary:
Bebop was born after hours. In the early 1940s, young musicians finishing their big-band gigs headed uptown to Minton's Playhouse and Monroe's Uptown House to jam, testing each other with blistering tempos and harmonies casual sitters-in couldn't follow. Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie emerged as the movement's twin engines: Parker with a torrent of melodic invention rooted deep in the blues, Gillespie with dazzling technique and the theoretical mind to explain it.

The new music was built for listening rather than dancing. Bands shrank to quintets, and melodies became jagged, quick-witted lines often written over the chords of familiar standards. Drummers like Kenny Clarke and Max Roach moved the beat to the ride cymbal and used the bass drum for accents, while pianists reinvented their role: Bud Powell with horn-like right-hand lines, Thelonious Monk with angular, deliberately placed dissonance.

52nd Street's tiny clubs became the scene's showroom, and the bop vocabulary of flatted fifths, double-time runs and altered chords became the grammar every serious jazz musician had to learn. Bebop recast the jazz player as an artist rather than an entertainer, and nearly every style that followed is either an extension of it or a reaction against it.

eras.name: Cool & West Coast
eras.tagline: Lower temperatures, lighter tones, West Coast sun
eras.summary:
If bebop was a sprint, cool jazz was a long exhale. It began with the nonet Miles Davis led in 1949 and 1950, arranged by Gil Evans, Gerry Mulligan, John Lewis and others. Those players explored soft dynamics, unusual colors like French horn and tuba, and the airy, vibrato-light tone Lester Young had pioneered. The results, later collected as Birth of the Cool, sounded closer to chamber music than to a jam session.

The approach found a natural home in California, where Mulligan's pianoless quartet with Chet Baker became a sensation in 1952. West Coast jazz favored counterpoint, crisp arrangements and a relaxed sense of space, much of it recorded for labels like Pacific Jazz and Contemporary. Back east, the Modern Jazz Quartet blended bop with Bach-like fugues, and Lennie Tristano's circle chased long, linear improvisations.

Cool reached the mainstream through Dave Brubeck, whose quartet with alto saxophonist Paul Desmond toured college campuses and, with Time Out, made a hit out of odd time signatures. The style is sometimes dismissed as polite, but its ideas of orchestral color, restraint and structure shaped everything from modal jazz to the ECM aesthetic.

eras.name: Hard Bop
eras.tagline: Bebop gets the blues, gospel and a heavier groove
eras.summary:
By the mid-1950s, a wave of mostly East Coast musicians wanted to reconnect bebop's sophistication with the church and the juke joint. Hard bop kept the quintet format and the dazzling technique but leaned on the blues, gospel harmony and a heavier, driving rhythm. Horace Silver and Art Blakey, co-founders of the original Jazz Messengers, set the template: catchy, riff-based heads, preaching solos and drums that pushed the band like a locomotive.

Blue Note Records, with Rudy Van Gelder engineering first in Hackensack and later in Englewood Cliffs, became the sound of the movement, while Prestige and Riverside documented a torrent of sessions. Clifford Brown and Max Roach co-led one of the era's great quintets until Brown's death in a 1956 car crash. Sonny Rollins made thematic improvisation an art, Cannonball Adderley brought joyous alto fire, and Charles Mingus wrote turbulent, gospel-drenched compositions that strained against form.

The Jazz Messengers in particular became a finishing school, cycling through Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard and, decades later, Wynton Marsalis. Hard bop is jazz at its most immediately satisfying: tough, soulful and swinging, and its tunes remain the core repertoire of jam sessions everywhere.

eras.name: Latin Jazz & Bossa Nova
eras.tagline: Clave, congas and the quiet storm of bossa nova
eras.summary:
Latin rhythms had flavored jazz since Jelly Roll Morton spoke of the 'Spanish tinge,' but the real fusion arrived in 1940s New York. Machito's Afro-Cubans, with musical director Mario Bauzá, paired a Cuban rhythm section with big-band jazz voicings, and in 1947 Dizzy Gillespie hired the Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo, whose congas on 'Manteca' helped give birth to Cubop. Through the 1950s the mambo craze turned the Palladium Ballroom into a temple, ruled by Machito, Tito Puente and Tito Rodríguez.

A gentler revolution came from Brazil. At the end of the 1950s, João Gilberto's hushed voice and syncopated guitar, setting songs by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes, launched bossa nova: samba slowed down, harmonically rich and intimate. American musicians took notice. Stan Getz and Charlie Byrd's Jazz Samba became a hit in 1962, and Getz/Gilberto, with Astrud Gilberto singing 'The Girl from Ipanema,' won the Grammy for Album of the Year.

Meanwhile percussionists like Mongo Santamaría carried Afro-Cuban grooves into soul and boogaloo, and Cuba itself would later produce virtuosos like Chucho Valdés. Latin jazz proved that jazz's rhythmic foundation could be rebuilt in many languages.

eras.name: Soul Jazz & the Organ Trio
eras.tagline: Hammond grooves, gospel fire and the jukebox
eras.summary:
Soul jazz took hard bop's gospel streak and turned it into a party. Its signature sound was the Hammond B-3 organ, which Jimmy Smith transformed from a roller-rink novelty into a roaring one-man orchestra, walking bass lines with his left hand and feet. Paired with a guitarist and a drummer, it formed the classic organ trio, and bars in Newark, Philadelphia and Harlem kept organs on their bandstands for a whole circuit of players, from Shirley Scott and Jack McDuff to Big John Patton.

The music was earthy and danceable: blues shapes, churchy amens, simple riffs and long grooves that built to shouting climaxes. It sold. Lee Morgan's 'The Sidewinder' and Cannonball Adderley's 'Mercy, Mercy, Mercy' crossed onto the pop charts, Ramsey Lewis scored with 'The In Crowd,' and labels like Blue Note, Prestige and Argo fed jukeboxes in Black neighborhoods across the country.

Soul jazz overlapped with R&B, Motown and boogaloo, and it embraced singers who moved between worlds, like Nina Simone. Purists sometimes looked down on it, but hip-hop producers did not: its breakbeats and organ vamps became some of the most sampled sounds in popular music.

eras.name: Modal Jazz
eras.tagline: Scales instead of chords, space instead of speed
eras.summary:
By the late 1950s, bebop's rapid chord changes had become a maze, and some musicians wanted out. Influenced by George Russell's theories, Miles Davis began building tunes on a single scale, or mode, held for many bars: first on 'Milestones' in 1958, then across Kind of Blue in 1959 with Bill Evans, John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley. Instead of racing through harmonies, soloists could stretch out, develop motifs and explore color.

The approach liberated the rhythm section. Coltrane's classic quartet with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones turned modal vamps into storms, with Tyner's ringing fourths and Jones's polyrhythmic swirl, on 'My Favorite Things' and 'Impressions.' Bill Evans's trio with Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian turned the piano trio into a three-way conversation.

In the mid-1960s, Miles's second great quintet with Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter and Tony Williams pushed further, stretching form and time until tunes seemed to breathe on their own. Blue Note documented a generation that grew up on these ideas, from Hancock's Maiden Voyage to Shorter's Speak No Evil and Tyner's The Real McCoy. Modal jazz opened a door that led straight to the spiritual, free and fusion movements.

eras.name: Free Jazz & the Avant-Garde
eras.tagline: Breaking the rules of chord, meter and form
eras.summary:
In November 1959 Ornette Coleman's quartet opened at the Five Spot in New York and split the jazz world in two. Coleman played a white plastic alto and dispensed with a piano, letting melody rather than chord changes steer the improvising. His album titles read like manifestos: The Shape of Jazz to Come, Change of the Century and Free Jazz, a collective improvisation for two quartets that gave the movement its name.

Others pushed in different directions. Cecil Taylor attacked the piano with the density of a modern classical composer. Albert Ayler played ecstatic, wide-vibrato hymns that sounded like a New Orleans funeral beamed in from another planet. Eric Dolphy found a vocabulary of leaps and cries that bridged inside and out, Sun Ra's Arkestra built an entire cosmology, and Coltrane himself, with Ascension in 1965, embraced the energy of the younger players.

The music became entwined with the Black Arts Movement, civil rights and self-determination. Musicians formed collectives like Chicago's AACM, released records on small labels such as ESP-Disk and staged concerts in lofts. Abrasive to some and liberating to others, free jazz proved that jazz could question its own rules, and its spirit still runs through improvised music worldwide.

eras.name: Spiritual Jazz
eras.tagline: Devotion, drones and the search for transcendence
eras.summary:
John Coltrane's A Love Supreme, recorded in December 1964, framed a jazz album as a prayer in four parts, and a generation took the hint. Spiritual jazz grew out of modal vamps and free-jazz intensity, but its goal was transcendence rather than confrontation. Musicians drew on African, Indian and Middle Eastern music, swapping standards for chants, drones, harps, bells and hand percussion.

After Coltrane's death in 1967, Alice Coltrane became one of the movement's visionaries, weaving harp and organ into devotional epics like Journey in Satchidananda. Pharoah Sanders, Coltrane's last saxophone partner, made 'The Creator Has a Master Plan' a thirty-minute-plus hymn of joy and fury. Impulse! Records gave this music a major-label home, while independent labels like Strata-East and Black Jazz let artists own their work.

Sun Ra's Arkestra preached Afrofuturist myth, Archie Shepp answered the Attica prison uprising with Attica Blues, and McCoy Tyner recorded sprawling, percussive suites for Milestone. Long out of fashion, the style was rediscovered by crate-diggers in the 1990s and 2000s, and it now echoes loudly in the work of Kamasi Washington, Shabaka Hutchings and the London scene.

eras.name: Fusion & Jazz-Rock
eras.tagline: Electric instruments, rock power and funk grooves
eras.summary:
By the late 1960s rock and soul were the sound of youth culture, and Miles Davis wanted in. He brought electric piano and guitar into his band, and with In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew, dense, studio-sculpted records shaped with producer Teo Macero, he blew the doors off. Bitches Brew became a gold record and a launch pad: a remarkable number of the musicians on those sessions went on to lead defining fusion bands.

Wayne Shorter and Joe Zawinul formed Weather Report, Chick Corea founded Return to Forever, and John McLaughlin's Mahavishnu Orchestra fused jazz improvisation with rock volume and Indian rhythmic complexity, while Tony Williams's Lifetime roared with organ and guitar. Herbie Hancock's Head Hunters married jazz to funk so effectively that it became one of the best-selling jazz albums ever. Synthesizers, wah-wah pedals and Jaco Pastorius's singing fretless bass became new voices.

Fusion filled arenas and later softened into smooth jazz, which made it a punching bag for critics. At its best, though, it was some of the most adventurous music of the 1970s, and on ECM, Pat Metheny and others refined electric jazz into something spacious and lyrical. Its fingerprints are all over neo-soul, jam bands and today's genre-blind players.

eras.name: Neo-Bop & the Young Lions
eras.tagline: Young lions, acoustic swing and the jazz tradition
eras.summary:
By the early 1980s, fusion's commercial glow had faded, and a wave of young musicians in sharp suits turned back to acoustic swing. The figurehead was Wynton Marsalis, a New Orleans trumpeter who came up through Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, signed with Columbia and in 1984 won Grammys in both jazz and classical categories. His early quintet, with brother Branford on saxophone, revived the intensity of Miles's 1960s band, and his advocacy helped build Jazz at Lincoln Center into an institution.

The Young Lions label covered a generation, including Roy Hargrove, Joshua Redman, Nicholas Payton and Christian McBride, who studied the masters and treated hard bop and post-bop as a living language. Major labels signed jazz artists again, and CD reissue programs made the classic catalog newly available. Not everyone agreed with the neoclassical emphasis, and debates about tradition versus innovation filled the magazines.

Other paths flourished alongside. Keith Jarrett's Standards Trio made the Great American Songbook sound freshly invented, Cassandra Wilson reimagined Delta blues and pop songs in dusky, atmospheric settings, and Brad Mehldau's trio brought Radiohead and Romantic-era harmony into the piano trio. The era rebuilt jazz's institutions and audience, setting the stage for the eclectic renaissance that followed.
eras.documentaryQuery: Wynton Marsalis young lions jazz 1980s documentary

eras.name: The New Jazz Renaissance
eras.tagline: Hip-hop, spiritual fire and a global new wave
eras.summary:
Twenty-first-century jazz refuses to stay in one room. Musicians raised on J Dilla and Radiohead as much as Coltrane treat genre as a palette, and the line between jazz, hip-hop, R&B and electronic music has never been thinner. Robert Glasper's Black Radio, which won the Grammy for Best R&B Album, pulled jazz harmony into neo-soul. Kamasi Washington's three-hour The Epic, arriving weeks after Kendrick Lamar's jazz-soaked To Pimp a Butterfly, proved that a young audience was hungry for big, spiritual sounds.

London became a second capital. A scene nurtured by community programs like Tomorrow's Warriors produced Shabaka Hutchings, Nubya Garcia, Ezra Collective and Moses Boyd, mixing jazz with grime, Afrobeat, dub and Caribbean rhythms. In Chicago, Makaya McCraven turned live improvisation into beat-tape collages. Out of New Orleans, Christian Scott aTunde Adjuah folded West African rhythm and trap drums into his stretch music, and Snarky Puppy built a global following for virtuosic, groove-heavy ensemble playing.

The tradition is in good hands, too. Cécile McLorin Salvant reimagines century-old songs with theatrical daring, Esperanza Spalding became the first jazz artist to win Best New Artist, and Brad Mehldau and Ambrose Akinmusire keep expanding what an acoustic group can say.

artists.blurb: The polyrhythmic engine of Coltrane's quartet played the drums like rolling surf, layering triplets and cross-rhythms into a churning, elemental swing.

artists.name: Ornette Coleman
artists.blurb: The Texan alto saxophonist who freed jazz from fixed chord changes, playing raw, vocal melodies that sounded both ancient and from the future.

artists.name: Cecil Taylor
artists.blurb: A pianist of volcanic energy who treated the keyboard like 88 tuned drums, building dense, cascading structures of sound unlike anything before.

artists.name: Albert Ayler
artists.blurb: Ayler played folk-like themes with a huge, quivering tenor sound and then shattered them into ecstatic cries, the most spiritual of the free players.

artists.name: Eric Dolphy
artists.blurb: A multi-instrumentalist on alto, flute and bass clarinet whose wide-interval leaps and vocal cries bridged hard bop and the avant-garde before his death at 36.

artists.name: Sun Ra
artists.blurb: A keyboardist and bandleader who claimed Saturn as his home, Sun Ra led his Arkestra through swing, space chants and electronic explorations, inventing Afrofuturism along the way.

artists.name: Don Cherry
artists.blurb: Ornette's pocket-trumpet partner became a globe-trotting pioneer of world music, folding African, Indian and Scandinavian sounds into free jazz.

artists.name: Archie Shepp
artists.blurb: A fiery tenor saxophonist, playwright and activist who fused free jazz with the blues and made his horn a voice for Black liberation.

artists.name: Alice Coltrane
artists.blurb: A pianist, harpist and organist who transformed her spiritual practice into cosmic, devotional music, among the most visionary in jazz.

artists.name: Pharoah Sanders
artists.blurb: Coltrane's last saxophone partner developed a sound that moved from terrifying overblown cries to tender, prayer-like melody, the voice of spiritual jazz.
signatureTracks: The Creator Has a Master Plan

artists.name: Chick Corea
artists.blurb: A prolific pianist and composer who moved from Miles's electric band to Return to Forever's Latin-tinged fusion, writing standards like 'Spain' along the way.
artists.videoQuery: Chick Corea Return to Forever live

artists.name: John McLaughlin
artists.blurb: An English guitarist whose ferocious speed and Indian-influenced spirituality powered Miles's electric records and the Mahavishnu Orchestra.

artists.name: Jaco Pastorius
artists.blurb: The self-proclaimed world's greatest bass player made a strong case. His fretless electric bass sang melodies, chords and harmonics, revolutionizing the instrument.

artists.name: Joe Zawinul
artists.blurb: An Austrian keyboardist who wrote 'Mercy, Mercy, Mercy' for Cannonball, shaped Miles's In a Silent Way and co-led Weather Report into synth-driven global grooves.

artists.name: Pat Metheny
artists.blurb: A Missouri guitarist with a warm, singing tone whose Pat Metheny Group crafted cinematic, melodic jazz and whose collaborations range from Ornette to Brad Mehldau.

artists.name: Wynton Marsalis
artists.blurb: A brilliant trumpeter, composer and educator who led the 1980s acoustic revival and became the music's most visible advocate as artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center.
artists.videoQuery: Wynton Marsalis live Jazz at Lincoln Center

artists.name: Keith Jarrett
artists.blurb: A pianist of rapturous lyricism, known for vast solo improvisations like The Köln Concert and a long-running Standards Trio that rethought the American songbook.

artists.name: Roy Hargrove
artists.blurb: A Texas trumpeter discovered by Wynton Marsalis who swung hard in the acoustic tradition, explored Cuban music with Crisol and funk with the RH Factor.

artists.name: Joshua Redman
artists.blurb: A Harvard graduate who won the 1991 Monk Competition and became the most celebrated tenor of his generation, with a warm, soulful sound and intellectual flair.

artists.name: Cassandra Wilson
artists.blurb: A Mississippi-born singer with a smoky contralto who reimagined Delta blues, pop and standards in earthy, atmospheric arrangements, redefining the jazz vocal album.

artists.name: Brad Mehldau
artists.blurb: The most influential jazz pianist of his generation folds Bach-like counterpoint, Romantic introspection and Radiohead covers into a deeply personal trio language.

artists.name: Kamasi Washington
artists.blurb: A Los Angeles tenor saxophonist whose epic, choir-and-strings albums revived spiritual jazz for a new generation and brought jazz back to rock festivals.

artists.name: Robert Glasper
artists.blurb: A Houston-born pianist who erased the line between jazz, hip-hop and neo-soul; his Black Radio albums made jazz harmony the backbone of modern R&B.

artists.name: Esperanza Spalding
artists.blurb: A bassist, singer and composer whose daring, genre-crossing projects run from Latin-inflected jazz to art-rock theater and opera with Wayne Shorter.

artists.name: Shabaka Hutchings
artists.blurb: The catalyst of London's jazz renaissance led Sons of Kemet, The Comet Is Coming and Shabaka and the Ancestors, before turning to flutes for a meditative new chapter.
signatureTracks: In the Castle of My Skin

artists.name: Cécile McLorin Salvant
artists.blurb: A singer of rare intelligence and theatrical range who unearths forgotten songs and reinterprets standards with wit, darkness and astonishing control.

artists.name: Makaya McCraven
artists.blurb: A Chicago drummer and producer who records live improvisations and edits them into hypnotic beat-driven collages, a self-described beat scientist.

artists.name: Christian Scott aTunde Adjuah
artists.blurb: A New Orleans trumpeter and Black Indian chief whose stretch music blends jazz with West African rhythm, trap drums and his own redesigned instruments.

artists.name: Snarky Puppy
artists.blurb: Bassist Michael League's sprawling collective, born at the University of North Texas, filmed its studio-with-audience sessions into a grassroots global phenomenon.

artists.name: Ambrose Akinmusire
artists.blurb: An Oakland trumpeter with a vulnerable, searching sound whose Blue Note albums mix jazz with poetry, chamber strings and protest songs.

artists.name: Nubya Garcia
artists.blurb: A London tenor saxophonist with a deep, rich tone whose music draws on dub, cumbia and Caribbean roots, a leading voice of the UK scene.

artists.name: Ron Carter
artists.blurb: The most recorded bassist in jazz history anchored Miles Davis's second great quintet and dozens of 1960s Blue Note dates with a deep, singing tone and a harmonic imagination that let the bass steer the band.

artists.name: Paul Chambers
artists.blurb: The bassist of choice in the hard-bop years, Chambers held down Miles Davis's rhythm section for eight years, from 'Round About Midnight to Kind of Blue, and was among the first to take bowed bass solos seriously.

artists.name: Charlie Haden
artists.blurb: Haden's warm, folk-rooted bass helped free the instrument in Ornette Coleman's quartet, moving with the soloist instead of marking the chords, and he later led the politically charged Liberation Music Orchestra.

artists.name: Richard Davis
artists.blurb: Equally at home with Eric Dolphy, Sarah Vaughan and symphony orchestras, Davis brought a classical player's range and an unpredictable swing to some of the most adventurous sessions of the 1960s.

artists.name: Jimmy Blanton
artists.blurb: In barely two years with Duke Ellington, before tuberculosis took him at 23, Blanton turned the bass from a timekeeper into a solo voice, with a big, melodic sound every modern bassist inherited.
artists.videoQuery: Jimmy Blanton Duke Ellington Jack the Bear

artists.name: Walter Page
artists.blurb: The anchor of Count Basie's "All-American Rhythm Section", Page brought the even, walking four-beat bass of his Kansas City Blue Devils that made the Basie band float.
artists.videoQuery: Count Basie Walter Page rhythm section

artists.name: Gary Peacock
artists.blurb: Peacock went from Albert Ayler's ecstatic free jazz to three decades as the elastic, conversational bassist of Keith Jarrett's Standards Trio.
artists.videoQuery: Keith Jarrett Gary Peacock Jack DeJohnette trio live

artists.name: Billy Higgins
artists.blurb: With a light touch and a constant smile, Higgins drummed on Ornette Coleman's first revolutionary records and then on hundreds of sessions, from The Sidewinder to Dexter Gordon's Go.

artists.name: Tony Williams
artists.blurb: Joining Miles Davis at 17, Williams broke up the beat with a restless, polyrhythmic drive that defined the second great quintet, then helped invent fusion with his band Lifetime.

artists.name: Jimmy Cobb
artists.blurb: The drummer on Kind of Blue kept impeccable, quietly swinging time for Miles Davis from 1958 to 1963, and was the last surviving musician from that session.

artists.name: Roy Haynes
artists.blurb: Nicknamed "Snap Crackle" for his crisp snare, Haynes played with Lester Young, Charlie Parker and Sarah Vaughan, then with John Coltrane and Chick Corea, in a career that lasted eight decades.

artists.name: Kenny Clarke
artists.blurb: At Minton's Playhouse, Clarke moved the beat from the hi-hat to the ride cymbal and dropped surprise "bombs" on the bass drum, inventing the language of bebop drumming; he later co-founded the Modern Jazz Quartet.

artists.name: Jack DeJohnette
artists.blurb: Equally at home in Miles Davis's electric bands and Keith Jarrett's Standards Trio, DeJohnette played drums as a colorist, with a fluid, cymbal-led sound that spanned free jazz, fusion and the standards.

artists.name: Baby Dodds
artists.blurb: Brother of clarinetist Johnny Dodds, Baby Dodds was the first great jazz drummer on record, varying his patterns with press rolls and accents behind King Oliver, Jelly Roll Morton and Louis Armstrong's Hot Seven.

artists.name: Wynton Kelly
artists.blurb: Kelly's bright, bluesy swing made him Miles Davis's pianist from 1959 to 1963 and one of the great accompanists in jazz; his one track on Kind of Blue, "Freddie Freeloader", is the bluesiest on the record.

artists.name: Tommy Flanagan
artists.blurb: A Detroit pianist of quiet elegance, Flanagan played on both Saxophone Colossus and Giant Steps and spent years as Ella Fitzgerald's accompanist.

artists.name: John Lewis
artists.blurb: Pianist in Dizzy Gillespie's big band and on Birth of the Cool, Lewis founded the Modern Jazz Quartet and blended bebop with Bach-like counterpoint, with an economy that made every note count.

artists.name: Earl Hines
artists.blurb: Hines's "trumpet-style" piano, its octave melodies punching through like a horn, transformed jazz piano on his 1928 records with Louis Armstrong; his big band later gave the young Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie a home.

artists.name: Lil Hardin Armstrong
artists.blurb: Pianist, composer and bandleader, Lil Hardin played in King Oliver's band, married Louis Armstrong and urged him to lead his own groups, and wrote "Struttin' with Some Barbecue" for the Hot Fives.

artists.name: J.J. Johnson
artists.blurb: Johnson proved the trombone could play bebop, matching the speed of Parker and Gillespie with a clean, almost valve-like articulation, and set the standard for the instrument for generations.

artists.name: Kid Ory
artists.blurb: The New Orleans bandleader who gave the young King Oliver and Louis Armstrong work, Ory perfected the "tailgate" trombone, sliding glissandos under the melody, on Armstrong's Hot Five records.

artists.name: Jimmy Knepper
artists.blurb: Knepper's agile, unusual lines were central to Charles Mingus's late-1950s bands, Mingus Ah Um included, and he later played in Gil Evans's orchestra and the Thad Jones–Mel Lewis band.
signatureTracks: Better Git It in Your Soul

artists.name: Milt Jackson
artists.blurb: "Bags" slowed the vibraphone's motor to make it sing, bringing a blues feeling to bebop with Dizzy Gillespie and Thelonious Monk and, for four decades, to the Modern Jazz Quartet.

artists.name: Bobby Hutcherson
artists.blurb: Hutcherson gave the vibraphone a modern, harmonically open voice on 1960s Blue Note records, from Eric Dolphy's Out to Lunch to Grant Green's Idle Moments and his own Components.

artists.name: Lionel Hampton
artists.blurb: The first jazz star of the vibraphone, Hampton played in Benny Goodman's racially integrated quartet and then led a roaring big band whose "Flying Home" pointed the way to rhythm and blues.

artists.name: Joe Henderson
artists.blurb: A tenor saxophonist with a sound all his own, mixing bebop agility with sly, searching phrases, Henderson was everywhere on Blue Note in the 1960s, from The Sidewinder to Song for My Father and The Real McCoy.

artists.name: Johnny Hodges
artists.blurb: Duke Ellington's lead alto for nearly four decades, Hodges had the most sensuous sound in jazz, gliding between notes on ballads like "Passion Flower" and "Prelude to a Kiss".

artists.name: Ben Webster
artists.blurb: With Coleman Hawkins and Lester Young, Webster was one of the three great tenors of the swing era; his breathy, growling solo on Ellington's "Cotton Tail" became a test piece for every saxophonist.

artists.name: Lee Konitz
artists.blurb: A student of Lennie Tristano and the alto voice of Birth of the Cool, Konitz offered a dry, light alternative to Charlie Parker and kept improvising with rare freedom for seventy years.

artists.name: Harry Carney
artists.blurb: Carney joined Duke Ellington at 17 and stayed for the rest of Ellington's life, giving the orchestra its deep, burnished bottom and making the baritone saxophone a solo instrument.

artists.name: Johnny Dodds
artists.blurb: The bluesy, piercing clarinet of King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band and Louis Armstrong's Hot Five, Dodds was the model New Orleans clarinetist of the 1920s.

artists.name: Bennie Maupin
artists.blurb: Maupin's dark bass clarinet threads through Miles Davis's Bitches Brew, and his saxophones and flutes shaped Herbie Hancock's Mwandishi band and Head Hunters.

artists.name: Cootie Williams
artists.blurb: Williams took over the growling plunger-mute trumpet in Duke Ellington's orchestra; Ellington wrote "Concerto for Cootie" to show it off before Williams left for Benny Goodman's band in 1940.

artists.name: Buck Clayton
artists.blurb: Count Basie's lyrical trumpet star of the late 1930s, Clayton played with clean, singing phrasing on Basie's Decca records and on Billie Holiday and Lester Young's small-group classics.

artists.name: Harry "Sweets" Edison
artists.blurb: Edison's sly, muted trumpet earned him the nickname "Sweets" in Count Basie's band, and later made him Hollywood's favorite accompanist for singers, Frank Sinatra above all.

artists.name: Freddie Green
artists.blurb: For nearly fifty years Green strummed even, chunky chords in Count Basie's rhythm section, rarely soloing but giving the band its unmistakable pulse.

artists.name: Kenny Burrell
artists.blurb: A Detroit guitarist with a warm, blues-soaked sound, Burrell recorded for Blue Note, Prestige and Verve, most famously with organist Jimmy Smith and on his own Midnight Blue.

artists.name: Cándido
artists.blurb: A Havana-born conga player who moved to New York in 1946, Cándido pioneered playing several tuned congas at once and brought Afro-Cuban rhythm to records by Dizzy Gillespie, Machito and Billy Taylor.

artists.name: Don Alias
artists.blurb: Alias's congas and hand drums colored Miles Davis's Bitches Brew, where he also played the drum part on "Miles Runs the Voodoo Down", and Jaco Pastorius's debut album.

artists.name: Brandee Younger
artists.blurb: Younger carries forward the jazz harp of Alice Coltrane and Dorothy Ashby, and plays on Makaya McCraven's Universal Beings and Shabaka Hutchings's Perceive Its Beauty, Acknowledge Its Grace.

artists.name: Elena Pinderhughes
artists.blurb: A flutist and singer who began touring as a teenager, Pinderhughes became a key voice in Chief Xian aTunde Adjuah's band and plays on Ambrose Akinmusire's The Imagined Savior Is Far Easier to Paint.

artists.name: Johnny Hartman
artists.blurb: A baritone of deep, unhurried warmth, Hartman sang in the Earl Hines and Dizzy Gillespie big bands before the 1963 ballad album with John Coltrane's quartet that he is remembered for. The Bridges of Madison County brought his voice back in 1995.
artists.videoQuery: Johnny Hartman My One and Only Love

artists.name: Kurt Elling
artists.blurb: A Chicago baritone who left divinity school one credit short of a degree to sing, Elling writes his own words to improvised solos in the vocalese tradition and scats with a four-octave range.

artists.name: Bobby McFerrin
artists.blurb: McFerrin switches between bass line, melody and vocal percussion so quickly that one voice sounds like a band. He took the idea from solo jazz concerts to number one in 1988 with 'Don't Worry, Be Happy', the only a cappella song to top the US chart.

artists.name: Leon Thomas
artists.blurb: A singer from East St. Louis who passed briefly through Count Basie's band, Thomas found his voice with Pharoah Sanders: on 'The Creator Has a Master Plan' his chants and sudden yodels turn the voice into another horn.
signatureTracks: The Creator Has a Master Plan (Peace)
artists.videoQuery: Leon Thomas The Creator Has a Master Plan

artists.name: Les McCann
artists.blurb: A pianist and singer who built soul jazz on gospel chords and a shouting good humour, McCann had a million-selling hit at Montreux in 1969 with 'Compared to What', a protest song he sang over a churning groove. Hip-hop producers have sampled his records widely.
artists.videoQuery: Les McCann Eddie Harris Compared to What Montreux

artists.name: Shirley Scott
artists.blurb: Philadelphia's 'Queen of the Organ' mixed bebop lines with blues and gospel chords, first in Eddie 'Lockjaw' Davis's band and then on a long run of records with her husband, the tenor saxophonist Stanley Turrentine.

artists.name: Larry Young
artists.blurb: A Newark organist who began in Jimmy Smith's soul-jazz mould, Young took the Hammond B-3 into Coltrane's modal territory on Unity and then lent its roar to the first fusion bands: Tony Williams's Lifetime and Miles Davis's Bitches Brew.
signatureTracks: Softly, as in a Morning Sunrise

artists.name: Lou Donaldson
artists.blurb: An alto player who started out as a disciple of Charlie Parker, on Art Blakey's A Night at Birdland among other sessions, Donaldson settled into bluesy, danceable soul jazz with organ bands, from Jimmy Smith's The Sermon! to his own Alligator Bogaloo.

artists.name: Stanley Turrentine
artists.blurb: Mr. T's big, blues-soaked tenor came out of R&B with Earl Bostic and found its home in soul jazz: organ sessions for Blue Note with Jimmy Smith and with his wife Shirley Scott, then the polished CTI sound of Sugar.

artists.name: Dorothy Ashby
artists.blurb: A Detroit harpist who showed the instrument could play bebop lines as nimbly as a saxophone, Ashby later set it inside Chicago soul arrangements and the Japanese koto; producers from Pete Rock to J Dilla have sampled her records.

artists.name: Lonnie Liston Smith
artists.blurb: The pianist on Pharoah Sanders's Karma and Thembi, where he first played a Fender Rhodes, Smith joined Miles Davis's electric band and then led the Cosmic Echoes, whose floating, groove-based spiritual jazz drew a crossover audience.
signatureTracks: Let Us Go Into the House of the Lord
artists.videoQuery: Lonnie Liston Smith Cosmic Echoes live

artists.name: Charles Lloyd
artists.blurb: A Memphis tenor and flute player whose 1966 quartet with Keith Jarrett and Jack DeJohnette won over rock audiences with Forest Flower, Lloyd withdrew to Big Sur in the 1970s and came back with a searching, hymn-like sound, most of it recorded for ECM.

artists.name: Abdullah Ibrahim
artists.blurb: A Cape Town pianist first known as Dollar Brand, Ibrahim joined traditional African songs and the hymns of Cape Town's churches to the influence of Ellington and Monk. Ellington set up a recording session for his trio in 1963, and his 'Mannenberg' became an anthem of the struggle against apartheid.

artists.name: Mulatu Astatke
artists.blurb: The father of Ethio-jazz set Ethiopian modes over jazz and Latin rhythms on vibraphone and congas, instruments he brought into Ethiopian popular music. Berklee's first African student, he found a new audience when Jim Jarmusch used his music in Broken Flowers.

artists.name: Hiromi
artists.blurb: A pianist from Hamamatsu whom Chick Corea invited on stage when she was 17, Hiromi studied at Berklee under the wing of Ahmad Jamal and plays with a speed and theatrical force that runs from stride to progressive rock.

artists.name: Jan Garbarek
artists.blurb: A Norwegian saxophonist with a keening, glacial tone, Garbarek became one of the voices most associated with ECM, in Keith Jarrett's European Quartet and his own groups; Officium, with the Hilliard Ensemble's early music, reached pop charts across Europe.

artists.name: Tomasz Stańko
artists.blurb: A Polish trumpeter whose early-1960s Jazz Darings are often called the first European free-jazz group, Stańko played on Krzysztof Komeda's Astigmatic, joined Cecil Taylor's big band and late in life made dark, lyrical ECM records with young Polish players.

artists.name: Esbjörn Svensson
artists.blurb: The Swedish pianist's trio e.s.t. gave acoustic jazz rock dynamics, electronics and pop melody, and drew crowds few jazz groups reach; in 2006 it became the first European band on DownBeat's cover. Svensson died in a diving accident in 2008.

artists.name: Courtney Pine
artists.blurb: A London saxophonist who founded the Jazz Warriors, a big band of young Black British musicians, in 1985, Pine took his debut into the UK top 40 and mixed post-bop with reggae and soul, a forerunner of the London scene that followed.

artists.name: Egberto Gismonti
artists.blurb: A self-taught Brazilian guitarist who plays eight- and ten-string instruments as well as piano, Gismonti drew on time spent with the peoples of the Xingu in the Amazon; his ECM records with Naná Vasconcelos and with Charlie Haden and Jan Garbarek made him known abroad.

artists.name: Arturo Sandoval
artists.blurb: A Cuban trumpeter of blazing range and a founder member of Irakere, Sandoval met Dizzy Gillespie in 1977; Gillespie became his mentor and helped him defect while they toured with the United Nation Orchestra. His story was filmed as For Love or Country.

artists.name: Dave Holland
artists.blurb: An English bassist whom Miles Davis heard at Ronnie Scott's in 1968 and hired for In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew, Holland went on to Circle, his own Conference of the Birds and, from the 1980s, bands built on supple, grooving counterpoint.

artists.name: Jason Moran
artists.blurb: A Houston pianist whose trio The Bandwagon threads stride, Brahms, hip-hop and recorded speech through the same set, Moran also plays in Charles Lloyd's quartet and was named a MacArthur Fellow in 2010.

artists.name: Vijay Iyer
artists.blurb: A pianist who studied physics before he turned to music, Iyer builds trio music from interlocking rhythmic cycles and covers that run from Andrew Hill to M.I.A.; he was named a MacArthur Fellow in 2013.

artists.name: Medeski Martin & Wood
artists.blurb: A Brooklyn trio formed in 1991, MMW took the Hammond grooves of soul jazz into funk, hip-hop and free improvisation, with John Medeski on organ, Chris Wood on bass and Billy Martin on drums, and found its audience on the jam-band circuit.

artists.name: Original Dixieland Jass Band
artists.blurb: A quintet of New Orleans players, several from Papa Jack Laine's bands, who made the first jazz record ever issued, "Livery Stable Blues", for Victor in 1917. Their brash, tightly drilled ensemble sold widely, and their "Tiger Rag" became one of the most covered tunes in early jazz.
artists.videoQuery: Original Dixieland Jazz Band Livery Stable Blues 1917

artists.name: James Reese Europe
artists.blurb: Founder of Harlem's Clef Club and bandleader to the dancers Vernon and Irene Castle, Europe took the 369th Infantry "Hellfighters" band across France in 1918. The records it made in 1919, weeks before he was killed, catch ragtime and the blues on their way to becoming jazz.

artists.name: Blind Lemon Jefferson
artists.blurb: The "Father of the Texas blues" sang in a high, carrying voice over fast guitar lines that changed shape from verse to verse. His Paramount records of 1926 to 1929 made him one of the best-selling blues artists of the decade, and one of the first men to succeed on record as a solo singer-guitarist.
signatureTracks: See That My Grave Is Kept Clean

artists.name: Lonnie Johnson
artists.blurb: A New Orleans-born singer and guitarist whose single-note solos of the late 1920s, on his own OKeh records and as a guest with Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Duke Ellington, helped set the pattern for jazz and blues guitar. Two decades later he had a million-selling ballad, "Tomorrow Night".

artists.name: Robert Johnson
artists.blurb: A Mississippi Delta singer and guitarist who left 29 songs from two sessions in 1936 and 1937, sung over guitar parts so full they can sound like two players. Barely known in his lifetime, he became the most studied name in country blues once rock musicians took up his songs.

artists.name: Fletcher Henderson
artists.blurb: Henderson's New York orchestra, with Louis Armstrong in 1924 and 1925, Coleman Hawkins on tenor and Don Redman's arrangements, worked out how a big band could swing. When it broke up in 1934 he sold arrangements to Benny Goodman, and later joined him as pianist and arranger.

artists.name: Artie Shaw
artists.blurb: Shaw's clarinet rose clean and high over his band, and his 1938 "Begin the Beguine" made him one of the biggest stars of the swing era. He hired Billie Holiday as his singer that year, added strings and a harpsichord-led small group, the Gramercy Five, and quit music for good in 1954.

artists.name: Red Norvo
artists.blurb: Norvo brought the xylophone and marimba into jazz in the 1930s, when he and his wife, singer Mildred Bailey, were billed as "Mr. and Mrs. Swing". On vibraphone he kept moving: a 1945 session with Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, then a drummerless trio with Tal Farlow and Charles Mingus.

artists.name: Fats Navarro
artists.blurb: Navarro played bebop trumpet with a full, round tone and long, evenly placed lines, above all in Tadd Dameron's band of the late 1940s. He died of tuberculosis at 26, but Clifford Brown, Miles Davis and Lee Morgan all took something from him.

artists.name: Mary Lou Williams
artists.blurb: Pianist and chief arranger for Andy Kirk's Clouds of Joy, Williams also wrote for Benny Goodman and Duke Ellington. In 1940s New York she was a friend and teacher to the young beboppers, Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell among them, and composed the twelve-part Zodiac Suite.

artists.name: Joel Ross
artists.blurb: A Chicago vibraphonist who started out on drums in his father's church, Ross leads the band Good Vibes, has recorded for Blue Note since his 2019 debut KingMaker, and plays on Makaya McCraven's records.

artists.name: Immanuel Wilkins
artists.blurb: A Philadelphia-raised alto saxophonist trained at Juilliard, Wilkins writes long, searching pieces that face American history head-on; his Blue Note debut, produced by Jason Moran, came out when he was 22, and in 2026 he received a MacArthur fellowship.

artists.name: Samara Joy
artists.blurb: A Bronx singer from a gospel family, Joy won the Sarah Vaughan vocal competition in 2019 and, with a warm, unhurried voice rooted in the standards, became in 2023 a rare jazz singer to win the Grammy for Best New Artist.
signatureTracks: Can't Get Out of This Mood

artists.name: Anat Cohen
artists.blurb: Born in Tel Aviv and based in New York, Cohen put the clarinet back at the front of modern jazz, moving between swing, Brazilian choro and chamber music; the Jazz Journalists Association named her clarinetist of the year every year from 2007 to 2023.

artists.name: Jimmy Giuffre
artists.blurb: A Texas-born clarinetist and saxophonist who wrote 'Four Brothers' for Woody Herman, Giuffre became a quiet radical of West Coast jazz: his trio with Jim Hall played soft, folk-tinged chamber music, and his 1961 trio with Paul Bley and Steve Swallow moved toward free improvisation.
artists.videoQuery: Jimmy Giuffre The Train and the River

artists.name: Cal Tjader
artists.blurb: Tjader drummed with Dave Brubeck before Afro-Cuban music took hold of him; his bands set cool, airy vibraphone over mambo and cha-cha rhythms, made him one of the most successful non-Latino musicians in Latin jazz, and won him a Grammy for La Onda Va Bien in 1980.

artists.name: Curtis Fuller
artists.blurb: A Detroit trombonist with a warm, rounded tone and bebop fluency, Fuller played on Coltrane's Blue Train, was the Jazztet's first trombonist and spent 1961 to 1965 in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers.

artists.name: Trombone Shorty
artists.blurb: Troy Andrews grew up in New Orleans' Tremé neighbourhood and was leading a band by age six; with Orleans Avenue he folds the city's brass-band and second-line rhythms into funk, rock and hip-hop.

artists.name: Jimmy McGriff
artists.blurb: A Philadelphia policeman turned organist who learned from Richard 'Groove' Holmes and Jimmy Smith, McGriff played a gritty, blues-heavy Hammond B-3; his 1962 instrumental of Ray Charles's 'I've Got a Woman' made the pop top 20.

artists.name: Dr. Lonnie Smith
artists.blurb: Raised near Buffalo in a family that sang gospel, Smith came to New York in 1965, played in George Benson's quartet and on Lou Donaldson's Blue Note dates, then led funky, groove-heavy organ records of his own; turbaned and styled Dr. Lonnie Smith, he kept recording until 2021.
artists.videoQuery: Dr. Lonnie Smith Hammond B3 live

artists.name: Joey DeFrancesco
artists.blurb: The son and grandson of jazz musicians from the Philadelphia area, DeFrancesco signed with Columbia at 16, toured Europe with Miles Davis and brought the Hammond B-3 to a new generation, playing bebop at speed on top of Jimmy Smith's blues.
signatureTracks: The Creator Has a Master Plan
In the Key of the Universe

artists.name: DOMi & JD BECK
artists.blurb: Keyboardist Domi Louna (born Domitille Degalle) from France and drummer JD Beck from the Dallas area met in 2018 and write tightly packed, harmonically dense music for the two of them; their debut drew Herbie Hancock and Thundercat in as guests and earned a Best New Artist Grammy nomination.

artists.name: Christian McBride
artists.blurb: A Philadelphia bassist who toured with Bobby Watson at 17 and played with Freddie Hubbard in his early twenties, McBride has appeared on more than 400 records, leads a big band and several small groups, and was the Newport Jazz Festival's artistic director from 2016 to 2025.

artists.name: Yussef Dayes
artists.blurb: A South London drummer whose playing draws on reggae, jungle and grime as much as jazz, Dayes came up in the Afrobeat-leaning United Vibrations, made Black Focus with keyboardist Kamaal Williams in 2016 and reached the UK top five with Tom Misch.

artists.name: Emma-Jean Thackray
artists.blurb: A Leeds trumpeter who started on cornet in Yorkshire brass bands, Thackray writes, sings, plays and produces her own records, mixing spiritual jazz with funk and dance music.

artists.name: Tigran Hamasyan
artists.blurb: Born in Gyumri, Armenia, Hamasyan won the Thelonious Monk piano competition in 2006 and built a style on Armenian folk melodies and modes, odd meters and, at times, the weight of progressive rock.

artists.name: Jazzmeia Horn
artists.blurb: A Dallas-born singer who won the Sarah Vaughan competition in 2013 and the Thelonious Monk competition in 2015, Horn sings standards and her own socially minded songs, and is often compared to Betty Carter and Sarah Vaughan.

albums.title: The Essential Bessie Smith
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: The Empress of the Blues at full power: two discs of Columbia sides, including duets with a young Louis Armstrong, sung with a force that needed no microphone.
highlights: Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out

albums.title: Ma Rainey
albums.label: Milestone
albums.why: A generous gathering of the Mother of the Blues' Paramount recordings: tough, funny and frank songs about love, work and freedom from the tent-show era.

albums.title: Snowy Morning Blues
albums.label: Decca
albums.why: Harlem stride in all its rolling, two-handed glory, from the showpiece 'Carolina Shout' to warm tributes to his student Fats Waller.

albums.title: The Complete Hot Five & Hot Seven Recordings
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: The most important small-group records in jazz. Here Armstrong turns the New Orleans ensemble into a launch pad for the improvising soloist, and invents swing along the way.

albums.title: Birth of the Hot
albums.label: Bluebird
albums.why: Morton's Red Hot Peppers sessions are tightly composed yet wildly alive, with breaks, stop-time and shifting textures that showed jazz could be arranged without losing its heat.

albums.title: Bix Beiderbecke, Vol. I - Singin' the Blues
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Bix's cornet rings like a struck bell on these late-1920s sides with Frankie Trumbauer, a cooler, more introspective alternative to Armstrong's fire.

albums.title: Never No Lament: The Blanton-Webster Band
albums.label: Bluebird
albums.why: Ellington's orchestra at its peak, propelled by bassist Jimmy Blanton and tenor Ben Webster, and featuring 'Ko-Ko,' 'Concerto for Cootie' and 'Take the "A" Train.'

albums.title: The Complete Decca Recordings
albums.label: Decca
albums.why: The young Basie band out of Kansas City, with Lester Young, Buck Clayton and the All-American Rhythm Section swinging lighter and harder than anyone.

albums.title: The Famous 1938 Carnegie Hall Jazz Concert
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: The night swing played America's most prestigious stage, with guests from the Basie and Ellington bands and a 'Sing, Sing, Sing' that brought the house down.

albums.title: The Commodore Master Takes
albums.label: Commodore
albums.why: Includes 'Strange Fruit,' the song Columbia wouldn't let her record, plus intimate small-group performances that capture Lady Day's phrasing at its most piercing.

albums.title: Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Cole Porter Song Book
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: The first of Ella's landmark Songbooks: Porter's witty, worldly songs sung with flawless diction, sly swing and Buddy Bregman's elegant arrangements.
highlights: I Get a Kick Out of You

albums.title: Body & Soul
albums.label: Bluebird
albums.why: Built around the 1939 masterpiece that rewrote the ballad solo, this set follows Hawk's huge tenor from swing into the bop years.

albums.title: Djangology
albums.label: Bluebird
albums.why: Django and Stéphane Grappelli reunited in Rome with a local rhythm section, revisiting their Hot Club repertoire with dazzling, bop-aware fire.

albums.title: The Complete Savoy & Dial Master Takes
albums.label: Savoy
albums.why: The bebop revolution in real time: Bird's 1945 to 1948 studio masters with Miles Davis, Dizzy Gillespie and Max Roach, including 'Ko-Ko' and 'Parker's Mood.'

albums.title: Jazz at Massey Hall
albums.artistName: Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Bud Powell, Max Roach & Charles Mingus
albums.label: Debut
albums.why: Bebop's all-star summit: Parker, Gillespie, Powell, Mingus and Roach together in Toronto for one incandescent night, often called the greatest jazz concert ever.

albums.title: Groovin' High
albums.label: Savoy
albums.why: Dizzy's mid-1940s small-group and big-band sides, several with Charlie Parker, are the clearest blueprint of what bebop sounded like at birth.

albums.title: Genius of Modern Music, Vol. 1
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Monk's first sessions as a leader introduced a body of tunes so original that the jazz world took a decade to catch up, including his first recording of ''Round Midnight.'

albums.title: The Amazing Bud Powell, Vol. 1
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Powell at his most incandescent, with the furious Latin-tinged 'Un Poco Loco' and a 1949 quintet featuring Fats Navarro and a teenage Sonny Rollins.

albums.title: Sarah Vaughan
albums.label: EmArcy
albums.why: Sassy meets Clifford Brown: a small-group vocal record where the singer and the trumpeter trade ideas like two bebop horn players.

albums.title: Birth of the Cool
albums.label: Capitol
albums.why: The nonet sessions that launched cool jazz, with Gil Evans and Gerry Mulligan arrangements for French horn and tuba that turned bebop into chamber music.

albums.title: Chet Baker Sings
albums.label: Pacific Jazz
albums.why: Baker's fragile, unadorned voice and trumpet made this the defining record of West Coast romance, and his 'My Funny Valentine' haunts to this day.

albums.title: Time Out
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: A pop-chart smash built on odd meters: 'Take Five' in 5/4, 'Blue Rondo à la Turk' in 9/8, and Paul Desmond's alto floating effortlessly over it all.

albums.title: Miles Ahead
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Miles's first full collaboration with Gil Evans, a seamless suite for flugelhorn and a jazz orchestra glowing with French horns and flutes.

albums.title: Out of the Cool
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Evans at his most atmospheric, with slow-burning grooves, shimmering colors and Elvin Jones on drums, on the record that helped launch Impulse!

albums.title: Moanin'
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Hard bop's definitive statement: Bobby Timmons's gospel call-and-response title track, Lee Morgan's brash trumpet and Blakey's thunder.

albums.title: Study in Brown
albums.label: EmArcy
albums.why: The Brown–Roach Quintet at full gallop, with Brownie's golden trumpet tearing through 'Cherokee' and swinging with impossible ease.

albums.title: Saxophone Colossus
albums.label: Prestige
albums.why: Rollins's masterpiece, from the calypso joy of 'St. Thomas' to 'Blue 7,' a solo so thematically developed it became a textbook example of improvisation.

albums.title: Somethin' Else
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Cannonball's date with Miles Davis as sideman, featuring a smoky, unforgettable 'Autumn Leaves' that is a perfect first taste of 1950s jazz.

albums.title: Go
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Dexter at his most big-toned, relaxed and swinging, with Sonny Clark's piano and the irresistible 'Cheese Cake.'
highlights: I Guess I'll Hang My Tears Out to Dry

albums.title: Mingus Ah Um
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Gospel shouts, Ellington tributes and political satire: Mingus's most accessible album, including the elegy 'Goodbye Pork Pie Hat' for Lester Young.
highlights: Better Git It in Your Soul

albums.title: Blue Train
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Coltrane's lone Blue Note date as a leader, with Lee Morgan and Curtis Fuller in a three-horn front line on a blues that became an anthem.

albums.title: Giant Steps
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: The Everest of harmonic improvisation: Coltrane's racing chord cycles on the title track, balanced by the tender ballad 'Naima.'

albums.title: Song for My Father
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Silver's tribute to his Cape Verdean father, with a bossa-tinged title groove and a Joe Henderson tenor solo that ranks among the era's best.

albums.title: Getz/Gilberto
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: The album that carried bossa nova around the world, with Jobim on piano, Astrud Gilberto's 'The Girl from Ipanema' and Getz's tenor at its most tender.

albums.title: Chega de Saudade
albums.label: Odeon
albums.why: Bossa nova's founding document: João's whispered voice and revolutionary guitar beat set to Jobim's arrangements, a quiet record that changed Brazilian music.

albums.title: Wave
albums.label: A&M
albums.why: Jobim as instrumentalist, with lush Claus Ogerman strings and breezy themes that became standards; elegant music for late-night listening.

albums.title: Dance Mania, Vol. 1
albums.label: RCA Victor
albums.why: The Palladium era bottled: a blazing mambo big band with Santitos Colón on vocals and Puente's timbales driving every chart.

albums.title: Kenya
albums.label: Roulette
albums.why: Machito's Afro-Cubans at their most jazz-forward, with Cannonball Adderley and Joe Newman soloing over hard-charging Afro-Cuban charts.

albums.title: Afro
albums.label: Norgran
albums.why: Dizzy's Afro-Cuban suite with a full Latin rhythm section, built around 'Manteca' and arranged by Chico O'Farrill.

albums.title: Watermelon Man
albums.label: Battle
albums.why: Mongo's congas turned Herbie Hancock's tune into a hit, kicking off a run of Latin-soul crossovers with an irresistible boogaloo feel.

albums.title: The Sermon!
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: A twenty-minute church-meeting blues jam with Lee Morgan, Lou Donaldson and Kenny Burrell, the organ trio expanded into a revival tent.

albums.title: Back at the Chicken Shack
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: The organ-trio sound in its purest form, with Stanley Turrentine's bluesy tenor and Kenny Burrell's guitar easing into a deep, after-hours groove.
highlights: When I Grow Too Old to Dream

albums.title: The Sidewinder
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Morgan's swaggering, boogaloo-flavored title track became one of Blue Note's biggest sellers, and the whole album crackles with streetwise confidence.

albums.title: Idle Moments
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: A late-night masterpiece with Joe Henderson and Bobby Hutcherson, whose fifteen-minute title track is the most relaxed and lyrical blues imaginable.

albums.title: Mercy, Mercy, Mercy! Live at "The Club"
albums.label: Capitol
albums.why: Recorded before a whooping audience, this set gave Cannonball a pop hit with Joe Zawinul's gospel-soaked title tune.

albums.title: Little Girl Blue
albums.label: Bethlehem
albums.why: Nina's debut reveals her singular blend of jazz, classical counterpoint and soul, and includes 'My Baby Just Cares for Me' and her hit 'I Loves You, Porgy.'
highlights: My Baby Just Cares for Me

albums.title: Kind of Blue
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: The best-selling jazz album of all time and the perfect starting point: modal sketches played by Miles, Coltrane, Cannonball and Bill Evans with unhurried grace.

albums.title: My Favorite Things
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: Coltrane's soprano turns a Broadway waltz into a hypnotic modal trance on his first studio album with McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones.

albums.title: Sunday at the Village Vanguard
albums.label: Riverside
albums.why: The Evans–LaFaro–Motian trio's telepathic final performance, recorded eleven days before LaFaro's death and a landmark of interactive improvisation.

albums.title: Maiden Voyage
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: An oceanic concept album whose suspended chords and floating rhythms became the model for post-bop composition.

albums.title: Speak No Evil
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Shorter's dark, mysterious tunes, played with Freddie Hubbard, Herbie Hancock and Elvin Jones, have the logic of fairy tales and the weight of standards.

albums.title: The Real McCoy
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Tyner's first statement after leaving Coltrane, with Joe Henderson and Elvin Jones, opening with the ferocious modal workout 'Passion Dance.'

albums.title: Miles Smiles
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: The second great quintet at its most elastic, with Shorter, Hancock, Carter and Williams bending time on 'Footprints' and 'Orbits.'

albums.title: The Shape of Jazz to Come
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: The title wasn't hype. Ornette's pianoless quartet with Don Cherry plays melodies freed from chord changes, and the aching 'Lonely Woman' still stops listeners cold.

albums.title: Spiritual Unity
albums.label: ESP-Disk
albums.why: Ayler's trio with Gary Peacock and Sunny Murray: folk-like themes exploding into ecstatic, vibrato-drenched cries, a cornerstone of the avant-garde.

albums.title: Out to Lunch!
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Dolphy's angular masterpiece, with vibraphone, a teenage Tony Williams and Freddie Hubbard, sounds like hard bop seen through a funhouse mirror.

albums.title: Unit Structures
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: A dense, exhilarating large-ensemble record where Taylor's piano storms set the architecture for collective improvisation on a grand scale.

albums.title: Fire Music
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Shepp's fiery tenor mixes free blowing, Ellington, bossa nova and an elegy for Malcolm X, the avant-garde with roots and a political edge.

albums.title: Complete Communion
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Two side-long suites in which Cherry and Gato Barbieri weave through themes and free improvisation with a joyful, conversational spirit.

albums.title: A Love Supreme
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Coltrane's four-part prayer with his classic quartet: chanted, searching and overwhelming, one of the most profound records ever made.

albums.title: Journey in Satchidananda
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Harp glissandi, tamboura drones and Pharoah Sanders's soprano create a meditative masterpiece inspired by Alice's spiritual teacher.

albums.title: Karma
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Dominated by the half-hour 'The Creator Has a Master Plan,' with Leon Thomas's yodeling vocals, a hymn that swings from serenity to fury and back.
highlights: The Creator Has a Master Plan

albums.title: Space Is the Place
albums.label: Blue Thumb
albums.why: The Arkestra's Afrofuturist manifesto, with chanted invitations to the cosmos, swirling synthesizers and joyful big-band chaos.

albums.title: Sahara
albums.label: Milestone
albums.why: Tyner plays piano, koto and flute on a thunderous, Africa-inspired suite, spiritual jazz with the force of a sandstorm.

albums.title: Bitches Brew
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: A dark, bubbling electric cauldron of rock rhythms and collective improvisation that launched the fusion era and a dozen careers.

albums.title: The Inner Mounting Flame
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: McLaughlin's searing guitar, Jerry Goodman's violin and Billy Cobham's drums in odd-meter overdrive: jazz-rock at maximum intensity.

albums.title: Return to Forever
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: Corea's airy, Brazilian-tinged electric piano with Flora Purim's voice and Airto's percussion, fusion at its sunniest and most lyrical.
highlights: What Game Shall We Play Today

albums.title: Head Hunters
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Herbie goes deep funk with clavinet, synth bass and an unstoppable groove on 'Chameleon,' one of the best-selling jazz albums ever.

albums.title: Jaco Pastorius
albums.label: Epic
albums.why: The debut that redefined the electric bass, from a breakneck 'Donna Lee' to the harmonics-only ballad 'Portrait of Tracy.'

albums.title: Bright Size Life
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: A 21-year-old Metheny with Jaco Pastorius and Bob Moses: open, airy and Midwestern, it invented a new kind of jazz guitar trio.

albums.title: Heavy Weather
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Weather Report's commercial peak, with Zawinul's synth orchestrations, Shorter's soprano, Jaco's bass and the irresistible 'Birdland.'

albums.title: Standards, Vol. 1
albums.artistName: Keith Jarrett, Gary Peacock & Jack DeJohnette
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: The debut of Jarrett's Standards Trio, which spent three decades proving that familiar songs could be improvised into something new every night.

albums.title: Black Codes (From the Underground)
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Wynton's quintet with Branford and Kenny Kirkland channels the mid-60s Miles quintet with fierce precision, the young lions' defining statement.

albums.title: Blue Light 'til Dawn
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Robert Johnson, Joni Mitchell and Van Morrison reimagined with acoustic guitars and hand percussion; a moody, earthy record that reinvented the jazz vocal album.
highlights: You Don't Know What Love Is

albums.title: Wish
albums.label: Warner Bros.
albums.why: Redman's second album pairs him with Pat Metheny, Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins, mixing originals, Ornette and pop with warm, grounded swing.

albums.title: The Art of the Trio, Vol. One
albums.label: Warner Bros.
albums.why: The first of Mehldau's influential trio series with Larry Grenadier and Jorge Rossy, introspective, contrapuntal and quietly radical.
highlights: I Didn't Know What Time It Was

albums.title: Habana
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: Hargrove's Crisol project, recorded with Cuban and American players including Chucho Valdés, joins bebop fire to Afro-Cuban rhythm and won a Grammy.

albums.title: Black Radio
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Jazz harmony meets neo-soul and hip-hop, with Erykah Badu, Lalah Hathaway and Meshell Ndegeocello guesting on a Grammy-winning crossover.

albums.title: WomanChild
albums.label: Mack Avenue
albums.why: A startling breakout album of rare and classic songs delivered with wit, theatrical daring and deep roots in Bessie Smith and Billie Holiday.

albums.title: The Imagined Savior Is Far Easier to Paint
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: An ambitious, emotionally raw album mixing quintet jazz, string quartet and vocal songs, anchored by Akinmusire's vulnerable trumpet.

albums.title: We Like It Here
albums.label: GroundUP
albums.why: Recorded live in front of a small audience in the Netherlands, it captures the band's virtuosic, funk-powered ensemble energy, including the epic 'Lingus.'

albums.title: The Epic
albums.label: Brainfeeder
albums.why: Three hours of choir, strings and roaring tenor that revived spiritual jazz for a generation raised on hip-hop and stadium rock.

albums.title: Emily's D+Evolution
albums.label: Concord
albums.why: Spalding's art-rock alter ego: knotty bass riffs, prog-funk guitar and theatrical songs that take jazz harmony somewhere entirely new.

albums.title: Perceive Its Beauty, Acknowledge Its Grace
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Shabaka sets down the saxophone for shakuhachi and wooden flutes on a hushed, meditative record with guests including Moses Sumney, Saul Williams, Floating Points and Laraaji.

albums.title: Universal Beings
albums.label: International Anthem
albums.why: Sessions in Chicago, New York, London and Los Angeles, edited into a hypnotic, beat-driven portrait of a global jazz community.

albums.title: Jazz Batá 2
albums.label: Mack Avenue
albums.why: Chucho revisits his 1972 trio concept of piano, bass and batá drums, with Yoruba ritual rhythms and dazzling Cuban pianism.

albums.title: Ancestral Recall
albums.label: Ropeadope
albums.why: Scott's most radical stretch-music statement layers West African and Native American rhythms, trap programming and spoken word under his blazing trumpet.

albums.title: Source
albums.label: Concord Jazz
albums.why: Garcia's full-length debut blends deep-toned tenor with dub, cumbia and Caribbean rhythms, a confident flagship for the new London jazz.

albums.title: John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Six ballads recorded in one day in March 1963, Coltrane's quartet playing quietly around Hartman's deep baritone; the album entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2013.

albums.title: Dedicated to You: Kurt Elling Sings the Music of Coltrane and Hartman
albums.label: Concord
albums.why: Recorded live at Lincoln Center, Elling's tribute to the Coltrane and Hartman album sings its ballads with a string quartet and Ernie Watts's tenor in Coltrane's place; it won the Grammy for best jazz vocal album.

albums.title: The Voice
albums.label: Elektra Musician
albums.why: Recorded alone on a German tour, with no band and no overdubs, the first jazz vocal album made that way: McFerrin plays every part himself, from the bass line of 'Blackbird' to a scat sprint through Charlie Parker's 'Donna Lee'.

albums.title: Spirits Known and Unknown
albums.label: Flying Dutchman
albums.why: Thomas's debut, with Pharoah Sanders under a pseudonym, Lonnie Liston Smith and Roy Haynes, returns to 'The Creator Has a Master Plan' and adds songs against the Vietnam War and for Malcolm X, sung in his chanting, yodelling style.
highlights: The Creator Has a Master Plan (Peace)

albums.title: Swiss Movement
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: A set at the 1969 Montreux festival by McCann's trio with Eddie Harris and trumpeter Benny Bailey; McCann's sung 'Compared to What', a protest song over a pounding groove, and the album both sold in the millions.
highlights: You Got It in Your Soulness

albums.title: Queen of the Organ
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Recorded live at the Front Room in Newark in 1964, Scott's quartet with Stanley Turrentine stretches out on standards and blues, her organ swinging between bebop runs and churchy chords.

albums.title: Unity
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: With Woody Shaw, Joe Henderson and Elvin Jones, Young turned the organ toward Coltrane's modal music: no soul-jazz shuffles, but fast, open themes like Shaw's 'Zoltan', which begins with a march from Kodály.
highlights: Softly, as in a Morning Sunrise

albums.title: Alligator Bogaloo
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: A 1967 organ-groove date with Lonnie Smith and a young George Benson; the title riff, made up in the studio to fill three spare minutes, was the track that sold the record.

albums.title: Sugar
albums.label: CTI
albums.why: Turrentine's first record for CTI, with Freddie Hubbard, George Benson and Ron Carter, sets his tenor in Creed Taylor's polished sound; the title track is a ten-minute slow-burning blues, and the band also takes on Coltrane's 'Impressions'.

albums.title: Afro-Harping
albums.label: Cadet
albums.why: Ashby's harp inside Richard Evans's orchestral Chicago soul arrangements, on her own tunes and film and pop songs of the day, joining jazz harp to the sound of Cadet's soul records.

albums.title: Astral Traveling
albums.artistName: Lonnie Liston Smith & The Cosmic Echoes
albums.label: Flying Dutchman
albums.why: Smith's first record as a leader floats electric piano, soprano saxophone, tabla and tamboura over gentle grooves; its title piece was first recorded on Pharoah Sanders's Thembi, the session where Smith first played electric piano.
highlights: Let Us Go Into the House of the Lord

albums.title: Rabo de Nube
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: A 2007 Basel concert by Lloyd's quartet with Jason Moran, Reuben Rogers and Eric Harland: long, incantatory pieces on tenor, alto flute and tárogató, ending with Silvio Rodríguez's song 'Rabo de Nube'.

albums.title: Water from an Ancient Well
albums.label: Blackhawk
albums.why: Ibrahim's septet, with three saxophones and trombone, plays his hymn-like Cape Town melodies in rich horn voicings, among them 'Mandela', 'The Wedding' and a return to 'Mannenberg'.

albums.title: Mulatu of Ethiopia
albums.label: Worthy
albums.why: Recorded in New York in 1972, the album sets Ethiopian melodies and rhythms against funk drums, horns and Mulatu's vibraphone, an early album-length statement of the Ethio-jazz he invented.

albums.title: Another Mind
albums.label: Telarc
albums.why: Hiromi's debut, co-produced by her mentor Ahmad Jamal before she had finished at Berklee, runs from the rock-tinged 'XYZ' to long, many-sectioned pieces played at startling speed.

albums.title: Witchi-Tai-To
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: Garbarek and Bobo Stenson's Nordic quartet turn tunes by Carla Bley, Don Cherry and Jim Pepper into slow-building, open-air improvisations, an early example of the spacious sound ECM became known for.

albums.title: Soul of Things
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: A thirteen-part suite played by Stańko with the young Polish trio of Marcin Wasilewski, Sławomir Kurkiewicz and Michał Miśkiewicz: slow, dark-toned trumpet ballads with room to breathe.

albums.title: Seven Days of Falling
albums.label: ACT
albums.why: Esbjörn Svensson's trio with Dan Berglund and Magnus Öström plays acoustic piano jazz with rock dynamics and studio effects; the album charted on both jazz and pop lists, rare for a jazz record.

albums.title: Journey to the Urge Within
albums.label: Island
albums.why: Pine's debut, made in London with players from his Jazz Warriors, mixes Coltrane-inspired soprano and tenor with a reggae-soul single, 'Children of the Ghetto', and reached the UK top 40.

albums.title: Dança das Cabeças
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: Two continuous suites for Gismonti's guitar, piano and wooden flutes and Naná Vasconcelos's berimbau, percussion and voice, drawn from his time in the Amazon; it won Germany's Grosser Deutscher Schallplattenpreis in 1977.

albums.title: Flight to Freedom
albums.label: GRP
albums.why: Made in New York after Sandoval left Cuba, the album runs from Danilo Pérez's title tune and Chick Corea's 'Psalm', with Corea at the piano, to 'Caribeño', which Sandoval sings, his high trumpet bright over all of it.

albums.title: Conference of the Birds
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: Holland's debut as a leader, with Sam Rivers and Anthony Braxton on reeds and flutes and Barry Altschul on percussion, moves between free improvisation and folk-like tunes; the title piece came from birdsong outside his London flat.

albums.title: The Bandwagon
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Live at the Village Vanguard in 2002, Moran's trio with Tarus Mateen and Nasheet Waits plays Brahms, Jaki Byard and Afrika Bambaataa's 'Planet Rock', and builds pieces around recorded voices, among them a Turkish phone call.

albums.title: Historicity
albums.label: ACT
albums.why: Iyer's trio with Stephan Crump and Marcus Gilmore recasts songs by M.I.A., Stevie Wonder, Andrew Hill and Leonard Bernstein in dense, interlocking rhythm; it was nominated for a Grammy.

albums.title: Shack-Man
albums.label: Gramavision
albums.why: Recorded in a solar-powered shack in Hawaii, MMW's breakthrough sets Medeski's Hammond, clavinet and Wurlitzer over Billy Martin's funk drums and Chris Wood's bass, soul-jazz grooves played with a jam band's looseness.
highlights: Is There Anybody Here That Love My Jesus

albums.title: Free Jazz
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: Recorded in one take in December 1960, two quartets improvising at once, one in each stereo channel: Coleman, Don Cherry, Scott LaFaro and Billy Higgins against Eric Dolphy, Freddie Hubbard, Charlie Haden and Ed Blackwell.

albums.title: Accelerando
albums.label: ACT
albums.why: Iyer's trio with Stephan Crump and Marcus Gilmore again, setting Michael Jackson's 'Human Nature', Flying Lotus and Heatwave's 'The Star of a Story' beside pieces by Herbie Nichols, Henry Threadgill and Ellington.

albums.title: Tutu
albums.label: Warner Bros.
albums.why: Named for Desmond Tutu, Davis's tribute was written and largely played by Marcus Miller on bass, synthesizers and drum programs, setting the muted trumpet in a glossy 1980s studio sound; it won Davis a Grammy.

albums.title: Future Shock
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Hancock's electro-funk record with Bill Laswell and Michael Beinhorn; Grand Mixer D.ST.'s scratching on 'Rockit' took hip-hop's turntable into a jazz musician's hit and onto MTV, an early instrumental hip-hop record.

albums.title: River: The Joni Letters
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: Hancock's tribute to Joni Mitchell, with Wayne Shorter and singers including Norah Jones, Tina Turner, Leonard Cohen and Mitchell herself, won the Grammy for album of the year, the first jazz album to do so since Getz/Gilberto.

albums.title: Footprints Live!
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: The first album by Shorter's quartet with Danilo Pérez, John Patitucci and Brian Blade, recorded at European festivals in 2001, turns old themes like 'Footprints' and 'JuJu' into open, constantly shifting group improvisation.

albums.title: Sound Grammar
albums.label: Sound Grammar
albums.why: A 2005 concert in Germany by Coleman's quartet with two bassists and his son Denardo on drums, revisiting old tunes under new names; it won the Pulitzer Prize for Music.

albums.title: Song X
albums.label: Geffen
albums.why: Metheny, a longtime admirer, brought Coleman to Geffen for three days of ferocious free playing with Charlie Haden, Jack DeJohnette and Denardo Coleman, guitar synthesizer and alto saxophone blending in harmolodic counterpoint.

albums.title: The State of the Tenor, Vol. 1
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Henderson at the Village Vanguard in November 1985 with only Ron Carter and Al Foster, no piano: long, searching solos on Monk, Ellington, Sam Rivers and his own 'Isotope', with the trio leaving him all the room he wants.

albums.title: Beyond the Missouri Sky (Short Stories)
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: Quiet duets for Haden's bass and Metheny's acoustic guitars on folk songs, film themes and originals; it won the Grammy for best jazz instrumental performance.

albums.title: Ptah, the El Daoud
albums.label: Impulse!
albums.why: Recorded in the basement studio of her Dix Hills home, with Pharoah Sanders and Joe Henderson on tenors and flutes, Ron Carter and Ben Riley: long modal pieces led by her piano and harp, named for Egyptian and Hindu deities.

albums.title: New Moon Daughter
