albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Wilson's low voice among acoustic guitars, cornet and percussion, singing 'Strange Fruit' beside songs by U2, Hank Williams and the Monkees; it topped the jazz chart and won a Grammy.

albums.title: Lush Life: The Music of Billy Strayhorn
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: Strayhorn songs played in shifting line-ups, from solo tenor to a quintet with Wynton Marsalis; a critical and commercial success that opened Henderson's Verve years, and its title track won him a Grammy.

albums.title: Blood on the Fields
albums.artistName: Wynton Marsalis & Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Marsalis's oratorio about slavery, sung by Cassandra Wilson, Jon Hendricks and Miles Griffith with the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra; it won the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 1997.

albums.title: Keystone 3
albums.label: Concord Jazz
albums.why: Blakey's Jazz Messengers live in San Francisco in 1982, with Wynton and Branford Marsalis in the front line: the band that schooled the decade's young lions in hard bop.

albums.title: Canvas
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Glasper's first album for a major label, a piano trio with guests Mark Turner and Bilal, whose hip-hop-shaped grooves and chords point to the Black Radio sound to come.

albums.title: The Köln Concert
albums.label: ECM
albums.why: A wholly improvised solo concert at the Cologne opera house in January 1975, played on the wrong, smaller piano; it became the best-selling solo album in jazz history.

albums.title: The 75th Anniversary
albums.label: Victor
albums.why: The band's Victor sides of 1917 to 1921, opening with "Livery Stable Blues", the first jazz record issued: cornet, clarinet and trombone locked in a loud, busy ensemble, with farmyard effects for novelty. Its own "Tiger Rag" and "Fidgety Feet" became Dixieland standards.

albums.title: James Reese Europe's 369th U.S. Infantry "Hell Fighters" Band (Remastered)
albums.label: Pathé
albums.why: The 24 sides Europe's army band recorded for Pathé in the spring of 1919, just back from France: a big brass-and-reed band playing W.C. Handy's blues and syncopated show tunes with a looseness that points toward jazz.

albums.title: King of the Country Blues
albums.label: Yazoo
albums.why: Yazoo's single-disc selection from Jefferson's 1926–29 records: a high, piercing voice over guitar that runs, stops and restarts at will, on songs like "Matchbox Blues" and "See That My Grave Is Kept Clean" that later blues and rock players kept returning to.
highlights: See That My Grave Is Kept Clean

albums.title: Steppin' On the Blues
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Nineteen OKeh sides from 1925 to 1932: low-down blues and risqué hokum, a duet with Victoria Spivey, and guitar showpieces like "6/88 Glide" whose clean single-note runs gave jazz guitarists a model.

albums.title: The Complete Recordings
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Johnson's 29 songs from San Antonio in 1936 and Dallas in 1937, with a dozen alternate takes. Released in 1990, this set sold more than a million copies and won a Grammy, bringing Delta blues to listeners who knew it only through the Rolling Stones and Eric Clapton.

albums.title: Editio Princeps
albums.label: Gennett
albums.why: The 1923 sessions that put New Orleans collective improvisation on record: Oliver's muted solo on "Dipper Mouth Blues", the young Louis Armstrong on second cornet, and Johnny and Baby Dodds and Lil Hardin in a band that moves as one.

albums.title: Fletcher Henderson and Louis Armstrong 1924-1925
albums.label: Timeless
albums.why: Louis Armstrong's year in Henderson's New York dance orchestra. His hot, swinging breaks cut through the arrangements, and Don Redman's "Sugar Foot Stomp", built on King Oliver's "Dipper Mouth Blues", shows New Orleans jazz being turned into big-band writing.

albums.title: Blue Clarinet Stomp - Complete Sessions 1928 & 1929
albums.label: Frog
albums.why: Dodds's Victor sessions of 1928 and 1929, in trio, washboard-band and small-band settings, with his brother Baby Dodds in the rhythm: the clarinet that drove King Oliver's and Armstrong's groups, heard as a leader with a thick, bluesy tone.

albums.title: Classic Earl Hines Sessions (1928-1945), Vol. 1 & 2
albums.label: Mosaic
albums.why: Mosaic's survey opens with Hines's four OKeh piano solos of December 1928, "57 Varieties" and "Caution Blues" among them, and goes on to the first records of the big band he led at Chicago's Grand Terrace.

albums.title: Kid Ory's Creole Jazz Band 1944/45
albums.label: Good Time Jazz
albums.why: The band put together around Ory for Orson Welles's 1944 radio show, with Mutt Carey on trumpet, recorded these sides for Nesuhi Ertegun's Crescent label: New Orleans ensemble jazz from one of its first players, with Ory's trombone sliding under the lead.

albums.title: Satchmo at Symphony Hall (Live)
albums.label: Decca
albums.why: Armstrong's new All Stars in Boston on 30 November 1947, months after he gave up his big band: Jack Teagarden's trombone and singing, Barney Bigard's clarinet and Sid Catlett's drums, in the small-band format he kept for the rest of his life.

albums.title: Dance Of The Octopus
albums.label: Hep
albums.why: The first 26 sides Norvo led, from 1933 to 1936: the hushed chamber jazz of "Dance of the Octopus" and Bix Beiderbecke's "In a Mist", with Benny Goodman on bass clarinet, then swing dates where his xylophone sits among players like Artie Shaw and Bunny Berigan.

albums.title: Piano Starts Here
albums.label: Columbia
albums.why: Tatum's first solo records, made in March 1933, beside a 1949 concert at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles: sixteen years apart, the same torrential runs, sudden key changes and stride left hand.

albums.title: If You Got to Ask, You Ain't Got It!
albums.label: Bluebird
albums.why: Three discs that show both sides of Waller: the singer who sent up pop songs with His Rhythm, and the stride pianist and organist of "Viper's Drag", "Smashin' Thirds" and "The Jitterbug Waltz".

albums.title: The Complete Victor Lionel Hampton Sessions, Vol. 1
albums.label: Victor
albums.why: From 1937, while still in Benny Goodman's quartet, Hampton led Victor pickup sessions with players borrowed from the big bands, Ellington's men among them, and put the vibraphone out front as a lead jazz voice.

albums.title: The Essential Artie Shaw
albums.label: Bluebird
albums.why: Two discs from Shaw's peak: "Begin the Beguine", the 1938 hit that made him a star, "Any Old Time" with Billie Holiday, the string-lined "Frenesi" and "Star Dust", and the Gramercy Five's harpsichord-flecked "Summit Ridge Drive".

albums.title: The "Kansas City" Sessions
albums.label: Commodore
albums.why: Commodore's Kansas City Five and Six dates of 1938 and 1944 gather Count Basie's men, Buck Clayton, Freddie Green and Walter Page among them, with Eddie Durham on early electric guitar; on "Pagin' the Devil" Young plays his rarely heard clarinet.
highlights: Way Down Yonder in New Orleans

albums.title: Zodiac Suite
albums.label: Asch
albums.why: Twelve short pieces, one for each sign and each dedicated to musician friends, recorded for Asch in 1945: stride, blues and impressionist harmony in a suite that looks from swing toward modern jazz.

albums.title: On Savoy: Dexter Gordon
albums.label: Savoy
albums.why: Gordon's Savoy sessions of 1945 to 1947, made as bebop took hold: a big, unhurried tenor sound out front on "Long Tall Dexter" and "Dexter Rides Again", with Bud Powell and Max Roach in the 1946 band and Tadd Dameron and Art Blakey in the 1947 one.

albums.title: The Complete RCA Victor Recordings
albums.label: RCA Victor
albums.why: Gillespie's RCA Victor years, centred on his 1947–49 big band. With the Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo it recorded "Cubana Be"/"Cubana Bop" and "Manteca", landmarks in joining bebop to Afro-Cuban rhythm.

albums.title: The Fabulous Fats Navarro, Vol. 1
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Blue Note sides from 1947 to 1949, led by Tadd Dameron's sextet: Navarro's full tone and long, even lines on "The Squirrel", "The Chase" and "Our Delight", bebop at its most melodic.

albums.title: In These Times
albums.label: International Anthem
albums.why: Pieced together over seven years from sessions in five studios and four live rooms, McCraven's suite edits a chamber band, with Brandee Younger's harp and Jeff Parker's guitar, into odd-metered, softly driving music that sounds composed and improvised at once.

albums.title: Fearless Movement
albums.label: Young
albums.why: Washington called it his dance album, meaning movement rather than the club; made after he became a father, it trades cosmic sprawl for earthbound grooves, with guests from Thundercat and George Clinton to André 3000.
highlights: Asha the First (feat. Thundercat, Taj Austin & Ras Austin)

albums.title: Ghost Song
albums.label: Nonesuch
albums.why: Salvant's first album for Nonesuch sets seven of her own songs beside Kate Bush's 'Wuthering Heights', a Sting ballad, Weill and Brecht, and a traditional ballad, moving between theatre song, folk and jazz with a singer's command of character.

albums.title: on the tender spot of every calloused moment
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: A spacious, searching quartet record with pianist Sam Harris, bassist Harish Raghavan and drummer Justin Brown; its bluesiest track, 'Roy', mourns Akinmusire's friend Roy Hargrove.
highlights: Blues (We measure the heart with a fist)

albums.title: nublues
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Ross's fourth Blue Note album turns to melody, ballads and the blues, with Immanuel Wilkins on alto, seven originals, and versions of Coltrane's 'Equinox' and 'Central Park West' and Monk's 'Evidence'.

albums.title: Omega
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Wilkins's debut, produced by Jason Moran, points an alto-led quartet at America's racial violence in pieces like 'Ferguson' and 'Mary Turner' and ends with a four-part suite; NPR's critics poll voted it the year's best debut.

albums.title: Linger Awhile
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: Standards and bebop tunes sung with guitarist Pasquale Grasso and a small band, including 'Nostalgia', for which she wrote words to Fats Navarro's line; it won the Grammy for Best Jazz Vocal Album in the year she was named Best New Artist.
highlights: Can't Get Out of This Mood

albums.title: Quartetinho
albums.label: Anzic
albums.why: Cohen's chamber quartet with Vitor Gonçalves on piano and accordion, James Shipp on vibraphone and Tal Mashiach on bass and guitar plays originals and pieces by Jobim and Gismonti in soft, many-coloured textures, her clarinet at the centre.

albums.title: NOT TiGHT
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: The duo's debut, released through Anderson .Paak's label with Blue Note, packs dense harmony and fast-shifting drum patterns into short tracks, with guests including Herbie Hancock, Thundercat, Snoop Dogg and Kurt Rosenwinkel; it was nominated for the Grammy for contemporary instrumental album.

albums.title: WHO ASKED?
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Their second album grew out of orchestrating their music for concerts with the Metropole Orkest: written out in full before a note was played, it adds a small classical ensemble and the duo's own singing to Domi's piano and Beck's drums.

albums.title: The Movement Revisited: A Musical Portrait of Four Icons
albums.label: Mack Avenue
albums.why: A suite for big band, gospel choir and narrators portraying Rosa Parks, Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali and Martin Luther King Jr.; first written in 1998, expanded with a finale on Barack Obama's election, and recorded in 2013.

albums.title: Black Classical Music
albums.label: Brownswood
albums.why: Dayes's first solo album runs across 19 tracks of jazz-funk, reggae, Afro-Cuban grooves and ballads, with guests including Shabaka Hutchings, Tom Misch and Chronixx; it won the Ivor Novello award for best album.
highlights: Black Classical Music (feat. Venna & Charlie Stacey)
Raisins Under the Sun (feat. Shabaka Hutchings)

albums.title: Yellow
albums.label: Movementt
albums.why: Thackray's self-released debut, which she wrote, produced and mixed herself, blends spiritual jazz, funk and dance music, her trumpet and voice set among choir and band; it topped the UK jazz chart and won Jazz FM's album of the year.

albums.title: StandArt
albums.label: Nonesuch
albums.why: Hamasyan's first album of standards, recorded in Los Angeles with bassist Matt Brewer and drummer Justin Brown, bends tunes like 'All the Things You Are' and Charlie Parker's 'Big Foot' through his own rhythmic sense, with Mark Turner, Joshua Redman and Ambrose Akinmusire as guests.
highlights: All the Things You Are (feat. Mark Turner)

albums.title: Dear Love
albums.artistName: Jazzmeia Horn and Her Noble Force
albums.label: Empress Legacy
albums.why: Horn's first big-band album, with her 15-piece Noble Force, on her own label; its Grammy nomination for large jazz ensemble album made her the first African-American woman vocalist nominated in that category.

albums.title: Fontessa
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: The Modern Jazz Quartet's first Atlantic album sets Milt Jackson's blues-rich vibes inside John Lewis's formal designs, above all the eleven-minute title suite modelled on the characters of the commedia dell'arte.

albums.title: The Jimmy Giuffre 3
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: Clarinet and saxophones, Jim Hall's guitar and Ralph Peña's bass, with no drummer: the trio plays what Giuffre called blues-based folk jazz, and its closer, 'The Train and the River', turns up in the Newport film Jazz on a Summer's Day.

albums.title: Lee Konitz With Warne Marsh
albums.label: Atlantic
albums.why: Two of Lennie Tristano's students, on alto and tenor, weave long, cool lines around each other over Oscar Pettiford's bass and Kenny Clarke's drums, on standards, Parker's 'Donna Lee' and Tristano's 'Two Not One'.

albums.title: Jazz Samba
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: Recorded in a Washington church hall after Charlie Byrd heard bossa nova on a 1961 tour of Brazil, this set of Brazilian tunes, with Getz's tenor floating over soft guitars, reached No. 1 on the Billboard album chart and started the American bossa nova craze.

albums.title: Soul Sauce
albums.label: Verve
albums.why: Tjader's vibes over Willie Bobo's and Armando Peraza's percussion, with Kenny Burrell and Donald Byrd sitting in; the title track, Gillespie and Chano Pozo's 'Guachi Guaro', got radio play and the album sold over 100,000 copies.

albums.title: Blues-ette
albums.label: Savoy
albums.why: A relaxed hard-bop quintet date where Fuller's trombone and Benny Golson's tenor sing in close harmony over Tommy Flanagan's piano, opening with Golson's 'Five Spot After Dark'.

albums.title: Backatown
albums.label: Verve Forecast
albums.why: Andrews's major-label debut, produced by Galactic's Ben Ellman, sets New Orleans brass and second-line beats inside funk and rock, with Allen Toussaint and Lenny Kravitz as guests; it was nominated for the Grammy for contemporary jazz album.
highlights: On Your Way Down (feat. Allen Toussaint)

albums.title: I've Got A Woman
albums.label: Sue
albums.why: Organ trio soul jazz built around McGriff's instrumental of Ray Charles's 'I've Got a Woman', a single that reached No. 20 on the pop chart and No. 5 R&B in 1962, with blues and standards played on a churchy, gritty Hammond.

albums.title: Think!
albums.label: Blue Note
albums.why: Smith's second album as a leader, cut for Blue Note in 1968 with Lee Morgan, David 'Fathead' Newman, guitarist Melvin Sparks and extra Latin percussion, turns Hugh Masekela's 'Son of Ice Bag' and Aretha Franklin's 'Think' into long organ grooves.

albums.title: In the Key of the Universe
albums.label: Mack Avenue
albums.why: DeFrancesco's turn to spiritual jazz, with Pharoah Sanders on three tracks including his own 'The Creator Has a Master Plan', came almost fifty years after Sanders's Karma and was nominated for the Grammy for jazz instrumental album.
highlights: The Creator Has a Master Plan
In the Key of the Universe

milestones.title: Buddy Bolden's band
milestones.detail: By the mid-1890s cornetist Buddy Bolden is loosening ragtime and blues into something new in New Orleans dance halls.

milestones.title: "Maple Leaf Rag" is published
milestones.detail: Scott Joplin publishes 'Maple Leaf Rag' in Sedalia, Missouri; it becomes ragtime's defining hit and a pianist's rite of passage.

milestones.title: The blues goes to print
milestones.detail: W.C. Handy's 'The Memphis Blues' helps carry the twelve-bar blues from Southern juke joints into published sheet music.

milestones.title: "Jazz" appears in print
milestones.detail: The word surfaces in a San Francisco newspaper as baseball slang for pep, before attaching itself to the music.

milestones.title: The first jazz record
milestones.detail: The Original Dixieland Jass Band records 'Livery Stable Blues' for Victor, and the disc becomes a nationwide sensation.

milestones.title: "Crazy Blues" sells big
milestones.detail: Mamie Smith's 'Crazy Blues' becomes a smash, proving a market for Black artists and launching the 'race records' industry.

milestones.title: King Oliver records
milestones.detail: King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, with second cornetist Louis Armstrong, records in Richmond, Indiana, preserving New Orleans ensemble style.

milestones.title: The Hot Five's first session
milestones.detail: Louis Armstrong cuts his first Hot Five sides in Chicago, the start of records that made the improvising soloist jazz's main event.

milestones.title: Ellington at the Cotton Club
milestones.detail: Duke Ellington's orchestra opens at Harlem's Cotton Club, and radio broadcasts make his 'jungle' sound famous nationwide.

milestones.title: "West End Blues"
milestones.detail: Armstrong's opening cadenza on 'West End Blues' announces jazz as an art capable of grandeur.

milestones.title: Swing explodes at the Palomar
milestones.detail: Benny Goodman's band electrifies the Palomar Ballroom in Los Angeles, a night often cited as the start of the Swing Era.

milestones.title: Jazz at Carnegie Hall
milestones.detail: Goodman's Carnegie Hall concert brings jazz, and an integrated bandstand, into America's temple of classical music.

milestones.title: Blue Note Records is founded
milestones.detail: German émigré Alfred Lion launches Blue Note in New York with a boogie-woogie piano session.

milestones.title: "Body and Soul"
milestones.detail: Coleman Hawkins records 'Body and Soul,' a ballad improvisation so harmonically bold that it became an unlikely hit.

milestones.title: Bebop's workshop at Minton's
milestones.detail: Thelonious Monk and Kenny Clarke anchor after-hours jams at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem, where bebop takes shape.

milestones.title: Bebop on record
milestones.detail: Charlie Parker's Savoy session yields 'Ko-Ko' and 'Now's the Time,' the bebop revolution captured at full speed.

milestones.title: Cubop is born
milestones.detail: Dizzy Gillespie's big band features Cuban conguero Chano Pozo; their 'Manteca' fuses bebop with Afro-Cuban rhythm.

milestones.title: The LP arrives
milestones.detail: Columbia introduces the 33 1/3 rpm long-playing record, freeing jazz from the three-minute limit of the 78.

milestones.title: Birth of the Cool sessions
milestones.detail: Miles Davis's nonet records the first of the sessions later collected as Birth of the Cool.

milestones.title: The first Newport Jazz Festival
milestones.detail: The Newport Jazz Festival debuts in Rhode Island, creating the template for the modern jazz festival.

milestones.title: Ellington's Newport triumph
milestones.detail: Paul Gonsalves's 27-chorus solo on 'Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue' sets Newport ablaze and revives Ellington's career.

milestones.title: Bossa nova's first record
milestones.detail: João Gilberto's single 'Chega de Saudade' introduces bossa nova's hushed voice and syncopated guitar.

milestones.title: Jazz's miracle year
milestones.detail: Kind of Blue, Time Out, Mingus Ah Um and The Shape of Jazz to Come all appear in a single astonishing year.

milestones.title: Bill Evans at the Vanguard
milestones.detail: Bill Evans's trio records live at the Village Vanguard; bassist Scott LaFaro dies in a car crash eleven days later.

milestones.title: Bossa nova conquers the world
milestones.detail: Getz/Gilberto and 'The Girl from Ipanema' turn bossa nova into a global phenomenon; the album wins Album of the Year.

milestones.title: A Love Supreme
milestones.detail: Coltrane releases A Love Supreme, a four-part devotional suite that redefines what a jazz album can be.

milestones.title: John Coltrane dies
milestones.detail: Coltrane dies at 40; his late music's spiritual search becomes a guiding light for the decade that follows.

milestones.title: ECM is founded
milestones.detail: Manfred Eicher starts ECM in Munich, building a pristine, spacious sound that reshapes European and American jazz.

milestones.title: Bitches Brew
milestones.detail: Miles Davis's Bitches Brew brings rock electricity to jazz and becomes his first gold record.

milestones.title: Head Hunters
milestones.detail: Herbie Hancock's Head Hunters fuses jazz and funk and becomes one of the best-selling jazz albums of all time.

milestones.title: The Köln Concert
milestones.detail: Keith Jarrett improvises a solo concert in Cologne on a substandard piano; the recording becomes a best-selling solo piano album.

milestones.title: Wynton's double Grammy
milestones.detail: Wynton Marsalis wins Grammys in both jazz and classical categories and becomes the face of a neo-traditional revival.

milestones.title: Jazz, a national treasure
milestones.detail: The U.S. Congress passes a resolution recognizing jazz as a rare and valuable American national treasure.

milestones.title: Ken Burns's Jazz
milestones.detail: Ken Burns's ten-part PBS documentary Jazz reaches millions and sparks fresh debate about how the music's story is told.

milestones.title: Herbie's Album of the Year
milestones.detail: Herbie Hancock's River: The Joni Letters wins Album of the Year, the first jazz album to do so since Getz/Gilberto.

milestones.title: Esperanza is Best New Artist
milestones.detail: Esperanza Spalding becomes the first jazz musician to win the Grammy for Best New Artist.

milestones.title: Black Radio wins R&B Grammy
milestones.detail: Robert Glasper Experiment's Black Radio wins Best R&B Album, crystallizing jazz's new fluency with hip-hop and soul.

milestones.title: The Epic
milestones.detail: Kamasi Washington's three-hour The Epic arrives weeks after To Pimp a Butterfly and ignites a new, young jazz audience.

milestones.title: We Out Here
milestones.detail: Brownswood's We Out Here compilation spotlights London's young jazz scene, featuring Nubya Garcia, Ezra Collective and Kokoroko.

milestones.title: Shabaka turns to the flute
milestones.detail: Shabaka Hutchings steps back from the saxophone and releases the flute-led Perceive Its Beauty, Acknowledge Its Grace.
